persons.name: James Kinzie

occupation.note: 'James Kinzie and family ... resided near Wentworth's tavern' in the list Andreas prints of the settlement's residents; he is a candidate at the 1833 town election and takes five votes. He built the Green Tree Tavern in 1833 and leased it, and he was surety on Mark Beaubien's ferry bond of 6 June 1831.

persons.note: A BUILDER OF TAVERNS RATHER THAN A KEEPER OF THEM, which is why his structure links are thin. Andreas has him building the Green Tree and leasing it to David Clock; Charles Butler in August 1833 lodged at a tavern on the west side of the South Branch 'erected by James Kinzie, but kept by a Mr. Crook (?)' - the question mark is Andreas's or Butler's, not this project's. He is a half-brother to John H. and Robert A. Kinzie. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Kinzie, James” (poll_1833_017, line 38); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kinzie, James” (tax_1833_061, line 113); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kinzie, James” (poll_1834_066, line 235). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kinzie' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

resident_research.evidence_for: Early Chicago civic/business histories distinguish James Kinzie from the other Kinzie men and connect him with Wolf Point, auctioneering and early town affairs. The pass keeps those identities separate rather than treating the surname as a household merge rule.

research_note: A HOUSEHOLD WITH A FAMILY IN THE SOURCE AND NO PEOPLE IN THE RECORD. Andreas's list says 'James Kinzie and family' and this parcel writes one person, because naming a wife or counting children on the strength of the word 'family' is the exact move the grade vocabulary forbids. THE HONEST READING OF THIS RECORD is that it stands for at least three or four people and can defend only one.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
